claim: Expression of attenuated diphtheria toxin (aDTA) from the melanopsin (Opn4) locus (Opn4aDTA) results in ablation of mostly the M1 ipRGCs and does so only at adult ages.
source: As we have published previously, expression of attenuated diphtheria toxin (aDTA) from the melanopsin (Opn4) locus (Opn4aDTA) results in ablation of mostly the M1 ipRGCs and does so only at adult ages (Güler et al., 2008) (Figure 1A,B,D,E).
evidence: Supported by citation to Güler et al., 2008 and reference to Figure 1A,B,D,E showing data

claim: A newly generated line expressing full-strength diphtheria toxin (DTA) (Opn4DTA) causes ablation of ipRGCs at early postnatal stages.
source: A newly generated line, expresses the full-strength version of diphtheria toxin (DTA) (Opn4DTA) and causes ablation of ipRGCs at early postnatal stages (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B

claim: In Opn4Cre/DTA; Z/AP mice, ipRGCs were reduced in number at birth.
source: In animals heterozygous for DTA and Cre (Opn4Cre/DTA; Z/AP mice; Supplementary file 1), ipRGCs were reduced in number at birth (Figure 1A,C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A,C

claim: Total ipRGC number declined until P14, when approximately 500 cells survived, and then remained constant thereafter through 1 year of age in Opn4Cre/DTA; Z/AP mice.
source: Total ipRGC number declined until P14, when approximately 500 cells survived, and then remained constant thereafter through 1year of age (Figure 1A,C and E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A,C and E

claim: At 6 months of age, about 75 M1 ipRGCs survived in Opn4LacZ/DTA mice.
source: Using the LacZ locus with the aDTA or DTA loci, we show that at 6 months of age, about 75 M1 ipRGCs survived in Opn4LacZ/DTA mice (Supplementary file 1), and consistent with our previous report, about 125 M1 ipRGCs survived in Opn4LacZ/aDTA mice (Güler et al., 2008) (Figure 1F; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1F and Supplementary file 1

claim: About 125 M1 ipRGCs survived in Opn4LacZ/aDTA mice at 6 months of age.
source: Using the LacZ locus with the aDTA or DTA loci, we show that at 6 months of age, about 75 M1 ipRGCs survived in Opn4LacZ/DTA mice (Supplementary file 1), and consistent with our previous report, about 125 M1 ipRGCs survived in Opn4LacZ/aDTA mice (Güler et al., 2008) (Figure 1F; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Güler et al., 2008 and data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Some ipRGCs that express high levels of melanopsin (M1s) can survive the presence of a single dose of the full strength DTA.
source: These results show that even some ipRGCs that express high levels of melanopsin (M1s) can survive the presence of a single dose of the full strength DTA.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that some M1 ipRGCs survive in DTA mice

claim: Sparse retinal fibers were found in the SCN of heterozygous DTA mice (Opn4DTA/+).
source: Sparse retinal fibers were found in the SCN of heterozygous DTA mice (Opn4DTA/+) as observed in Opn4Cre/DTA; Z/AP mice (Figure 1A) but these retinal fibers were entirely absent in Opn4DTA/DTA mice (Figure 1D) suggesting that Opn4DTA/DTA mice have more extensive ipRGC loss than Opn4DTA/+ mice.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A and 1D

claim: Retinal fibers were entirely absent in the SCN of Opn4DTA/DTA mice.
source: Sparse retinal fibers were found in the SCN of heterozygous DTA mice (Opn4DTA/+) as observed in Opn4Cre/DTA; Z/AP mice (Figure 1A) but these retinal fibers were entirely absent in Opn4DTA/DTA mice (Figure 1D) suggesting that Opn4DTA/DTA mice have more extensive ipRGC loss than Opn4DTA/+ mice.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Opn4DTA/DTA mice have more extensive ipRGC loss than Opn4DTA/+ mice.
source: Sparse retinal fibers were found in the SCN of heterozygous DTA mice (Opn4DTA/+) as observed in Opn4Cre/DTA; Z/AP mice (Figure 1A) but these retinal fibers were entirely absent in Opn4DTA/DTA mice (Figure 1D) suggesting that Opn4DTA/DTA mice have more extensive ipRGC loss than Opn4DTA/+ mice.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of SCN innervation patterns in Figure 1A and 1D

claim: General retinal structure appeared similar between wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA mice by hematoxylin and eosin staining and fluorescent staining for various retinal cell types.
source: Wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA mice appeared similar by these stains, and quantification of total retinal thickness, as well as the thickness of each of the retinal layers, based on hematoxylin and eosin staining showed no difference between wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,E–F and 1D

claim: There was no difference in the number of SMI-32-positive ganglion cells, Brn3a-positive ganglion cells, cones, and starburst amacrine cells between wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA mice.
source: We also counted the number of SMI-32-positive ganglion cells, Brn3a-positive ganglion cells, cones, and starburst amacrine cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–J). When we compared wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA mice, there was no difference in cell number of any of these cell types.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–J

claim: About 50% of SMI-32 positive ganglion cells are M4 ipRGCs.
source: It is relevant to mention that about 50% of SMI-32 positive ganglion cells are actually M4 ipRGCs (Estevez et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2014), which express lower levels of melanopsin compared to M1 ipRGCs (Ecker et al., 2010; Sexton et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Estevez et al., 2012 and Schmidt et al., 2014

claim: M4 ipRGCs express lower levels of melanopsin compared to M1 ipRGCs.
source: It is relevant to mention that about 50% of SMI-32 positive ganglion cells are actually M4 ipRGCs (Estevez et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2014), which express lower levels of melanopsin compared to M1 ipRGCs (Ecker et al., 2010; Sexton et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ecker et al., 2010 and Sexton et al., 2015

claim: Expression of two copies of DTA from the melanopsin locus does not kill all ipRGCs.
source: Thus, expression of two copies of DTA from the melanopsin locus does not even succeed in killing all ipRGCs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that SMI-32 positive cells (including M4 ipRGCs) survive in Opn4DTA/DTA mice

claim: There was no difference between wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA mice in the number of nuclei or neurons in the SCN.
source: To assess potential off target effects in relevant brain regions, we counted the total number of nuclei (based on DAPI staining) and the total number of neurons (identified by antibody staining for Hu) in the SCN of wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA mice. There was no difference between wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA mice in the number of nuclei or neurons when compared in total or section by section through the SCN (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: The total size of the dLGN was not different between wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA mice or among any other tested mouse lines.
source: Furthermore, the total size of the dLGN was also not different between wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA mice or among any other tested mouse lines (Figure 4—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4E

claim: DTA efficiently and selectively ablated ipRGCs at early postnatal ages.
source: These data combined demonstrate that DTA efficiently and selectively ablated ipRGCs at early postnatal ages.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data showing ipRGC loss without off-target effects

claim: Opn4LacZ/LacZ and wild-type mice showed normal photoentrainment, phase shifting (at CT16), and free-running periods.
source: Opn4LacZ/LacZ and wild-type mice showed normal photoentrainment, phase shifting (at CT16), and free-running periods (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A–C

claim: Opn4aDTA/aDTA mice were unable to photoentrain or phase shift and free-ran under all lighting conditions with a period comparable to controls.
source: As previously published, Opn4aDTA/aDTA mice were unable to photoentrain or phase shift and free-ran under all lighting conditions with a period comparable to controls (Güler et al., 2008) (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by citation to Güler et al., 2008 and data shown in Figure 2A–C

claim: Opn4DTA/+ mice photoentrained, phase shifted (at CT16), and free-ran in constant darkness with a normal circadian period.
source: Opn4DTA/+ mice photoentrained, phase shifted (at CT16), and free-ran in constant darkness with a normal circadian period (Figure 2A–C) indicating that residual retinal input to the SCN in heterozygotes is sufficient for circadian photoentrainment.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A–C

claim: Residual retinal input to the SCN in Opn4DTA/+ heterozygotes is sufficient for circadian photoentrainment.
source: Opn4DTA/+ mice photoentrained, phase shifted (at CT16), and free-ran in constant darkness with a normal circadian period (Figure 2A–C) indicating that residual retinal input to the SCN in heterozygotes is sufficient for circadian photoentrainment.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Opn4DTA/+ mice photoentrain normally despite partial ipRGC loss

claim: In Opn4DTA/LacZ mice, circadian responses to light were highly attenuated, with inconsistent entrainment and phase-shifting, and exhibited a free-running period comparable to control mice.
source: In these mice, circadian responses to light were highly attenuated, with inconsistent entrainment and phase-shifting, and exhibited a free-running period comparable to control mice (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Opn4DTA/DTA mice did not photoentrain and free-ran with an abnormally lengthened period.
source: Similar to Opn4aDTA/aDTA mice, Opn4DTA/DTA mice did not photoentrain; however, they free-ran with an abnormally lengthened period (Figure 2A,B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A,B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: Full-strength DTA, but not aDTA, kills ipRGCs during early development.
source: Because full-strength DTA, but not aDTA, kills ipRGCs during early development, these findings suggested the hypothesis that ipRGCs act during early postnatal ages to establish a normal circadian period length.
evidence: Inferred from the differential timing of ipRGC ablation between DTA and aDTA mice

claim: ipRGCs act during early postnatal ages to establish a normal circadian period length.
source: Because full-strength DTA, but not aDTA, kills ipRGCs during early development, these findings suggested the hypothesis that ipRGCs act during early postnatal ages to establish a normal circadian period length.
evidence: Hypothesis inferred from the observation that early but not late ipRGC ablation causes lengthened period

claim: Loss of ipRGC innervation does not drastically alter SCN development.
source: We performed a general examination of expression of transcription factors important for SCN development and a neuropeptide relevant for clock function to examine the SCN, and found no apparent disruption in the SCN of Opn4DTA/DTA mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). Thus, loss of ipRGC innervation does not drastically alter SCN development, and it is possible the lengthened period stems from a loss of direct ipRGC-dependent regulation of SCN neurons.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: The lengthened period in Opn4DTA/DTA mice may stem from a loss of direct ipRGC-dependent regulation of SCN neurons.
source: Thus, loss of ipRGC innervation does not drastically alter SCN development, and it is possible the lengthened period stems from a loss of direct ipRGC-dependent regulation of SCN neurons.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the lengthened period phenotype

claim: The lengthened period effect in Opn4DTA/DTA mice could be due to altered input from the intergeniculate leaflet (IGL), which also receives innervation by ipRGCs.
source: Alternatively, this effect could be due to altered input from the intergeniculate leaflet (IGL), which also receives innervation by ipRGCs.
evidence: Alternative speculative explanation for the lengthened period phenotype

claim: Mice enucleated at P0 exhibited a lengthened circadian period similar to Opn4DTA/DTA mice.
source: However, mice enucleated at P0 exhibited a lengthened circadian period similar to Opn4DTA/DTA mice, whereas mice enucleated at P60 phenocopied Opn4aDTA/aDTA mice exhibiting a period comparable to intact mice (Figure 2A–B,D–E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2D–E

claim: Mice enucleated at P60 exhibited a period comparable to intact mice.
source: However, mice enucleated at P0 exhibited a lengthened circadian period similar to Opn4DTA/DTA mice, whereas mice enucleated at P60 phenocopied Opn4aDTA/aDTA mice exhibiting a period comparable to intact mice (Figure 2A–B,D–E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2D–E

claim: Circadian period length has been shown to be stable in adult mice kept under constant darkness for 2 months.
source: Circadian period length has been shown to be stable in adult mice kept under constant darkness for 2 months (Campuzano et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Campuzano et al., 1999

claim: ipRGCs function postnatally to set the length of the circadian period.
source: Thus, these data corroborate results from Opn4DTA/DTA mice indicating that ipRGCs function postnatally to set the length of the circadian period.
evidence: Inferred from the enucleation experiments showing age-dependent effects on period length

claim: Most (9 of 16) dark-reared mice exhibited a longer intrinsic circadian period than mice raised in a 12:12-LD cycle.
source: While the phenotype was less penetrant than that the Opn4DTA/DTA mice and P0 enucleates, most (9 of 16) dark-reared mice exhibited a longer intrinsic circadian period than mice raised in a 12:12-LD cycle and this was stable for duration of our recordings (up to 60 days; Figure 3A,B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The lengthened period of dark-reared animals was comparable to that exhibited by mice enucleated at P0 and mice with early postnatal ablation of ipRGCs (Opn4DTA/DTA).
source: The lengthened period of the dark-reared animals was comparable to that exhibited by mice enucleated at P0 and mice with early postnatal ablation of ipRGCs (Opn4DTA/DTA) (Figures 2 and 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by comparison of data in Figures 2 and 3

claim: Light contributes to the process of establishing circadian period length in mammals.
source: It has been thought that the mammalian circadian period length was established independent of sensory input, but our data show that light contributes to this process.
evidence: Inferred from the dark-rearing experiments showing light-dependent effects on period length

claim: In zebrafish, light is required to initiate expression of clock genes and for generation of rhythms.
source: In zebrafish, it is known that light is required to initiate expression of clock genes and for generation of rhythms (Ben-Moshe et al., 2014; Kazimi and Cahill, 1999; Ziv et al., 2005); however, this is the first evidence to indicate that light is also required for mammalian clock maturation.
evidence: Supported by citations to Ben-Moshe et al., 2014; Kazimi and Cahill, 1999; Ziv et al., 2005

claim: This is the first evidence to indicate that light is required for mammalian clock maturation.
source: In zebrafish, it is known that light is required to initiate expression of clock genes and for generation of rhythms (Ben-Moshe et al., 2014; Kazimi and Cahill, 1999; Ziv et al., 2005); however, this is the first evidence to indicate that light is also required for mammalian clock maturation.
evidence: Claim about novelty of the finding based on the experimental results

claim: Upon exposure to a 12:12-LD-cycle, dark-reared mice photoentrained, and light exposure during photoentrainment was sufficient to normalize the circadian period length.
source: Upon exposure to a 12:12-LD-cycle, dark-reared mice photoentrained, and light exposure during photoentrainment was sufficient to normalize the circadian period length (Figure 3A,B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: A single short light pulse (3 hr), which did not cause photoentrainment, was sufficient to set the circadian period of dark-reared animals.
source: Furthermore, a single short light pulse (3 hr), which did not cause photoentrainment, (Figure 3C,D) was also sufficient to set the circadian period of dark-reared animals (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C,D

claim: Brief light exposure is sufficient to set the circadian period and can occur in adults.
source: These data indicate that brief light exposure is sufficient to set the circadian period and can even occur in adults, thus, indicating a lack of a critical developmental window for this process.
evidence: Inferred from the light pulse experiments showing period normalization in adult dark-reared mice

claim: There is no critical developmental window for light to set the circadian period.
source: These data indicate that brief light exposure is sufficient to set the circadian period and can even occur in adults, thus, indicating a lack of a critical developmental window for this process.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that adult light exposure can normalize period in dark-reared mice

claim: By P7, ipRGCs have reached their central targets in the brain.
source: By P7, ipRGCs have reached their central targets in the brain (Figure 1A–B) (McNeill et al., 2011) and a subset of ipRGCs forms intra-retinal collateral axons that terminate in the inner plexiform layer, where they synapse onto dopaminergic amacrine cells (Joo et al., 2013; Prigge et al., 2016) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to McNeill et al., 2011 and data shown in Figure 1A–B

claim: A subset of ipRGCs forms intra-retinal collateral axons that terminate in the inner plexiform layer, where they synapse onto dopaminergic amacrine cells.
source: By P7, ipRGCs have reached their central targets in the brain (Figure 1A–B) (McNeill et al., 2011) and a subset of ipRGCs forms intra-retinal collateral axons that terminate in the inner plexiform layer, where they synapse onto dopaminergic amacrine cells (Joo et al., 2013; Prigge et al., 2016) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to Joo et al., 2013 and Prigge et al., 2016, and data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: P7 is in the middle of a critical developmental period for the image-forming visual system.
source: P7 is in the middle of a critical developmental period for the image-forming visual system.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about visual system development

claim: From P0-P14, the retinotopic map is being refined by spontaneously generated neural activity in the retina, termed retinal waves.
source: From P0-P14, the retinotopic map is being refined by spontaneously generated neural activity in the retina, termed retinal waves (Ackman et al., 2012; Feller, 2009; Feller et al., 1996; McLaughlin et al., 2003; Meister et al., 1991; Ramoa et al., 1989; Shatz, 1990; Stellwagen and Shatz, 2002; Xu et al. 2011; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work on retinal waves

claim: The presence of intra-retinal collaterals on ipRGCs at early postnatal ages provides anatomical means for ipRGCs to influence the retina during an important developmental window.
source: The presence of intra-retinal collaterals on ipRGCs at early postnatal ages provides anatomical means for ipRGCs to influence the retina during an important developmental window.
evidence: Inferred from the anatomical observation of intra-retinal collaterals and the timing of visual system development

claim: While retinal innervation of the superior colliculus in Opn4DTA/DTA mice was comparable to wild-type, eye-specific axonal segregation in the dLGN was severely disrupted.
source: To investigate this, we traced the axonal projections of retinal ganglion cells in adult wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA mice, and observed that, while retinal innervation of the superior colliculus in Opn4DTA/DTA mice was comparable to wild-type (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), eye-specific axonal segregation in the dLGN was severely disrupted (Figure 4A,B; Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Figure 4A,B

claim: In Opn4DTA/DTA mice, the ipsilateral zone in the dLGN had poorly defined boundaries and substantial contralateral innervation.
source: In Opn4DTA/DTA mice, the ipsilateral zone had poorly defined boundaries and substantial contralateral innervation (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4A

claim: In Opn4DTA/DTA mice, there was a significant increase in the percentage of pixels with overlapping input from the two eyes in the dLGN.
source: In Opn4DTA/DTA mice, there was a significant increase in the percentage of pixels with overlapping input from the two eyes, and this eye-specific segregation defect was most severe in the caudal dLGN (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 4F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 4F

claim: The eye-specific segregation defect in Opn4DTA/DTA mice was most severe in the caudal dLGN.
source: In Opn4DTA/DTA mice, there was a significant increase in the percentage of pixels with overlapping input from the two eyes, and this eye-specific segregation defect was most severe in the caudal dLGN (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 4F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 4F

claim: The total amount of ipsilateral and contralateral input and total dLGN size were similar across all tested genotypes.
source: The total amount of ipsilateral and contralateral input and total dLGN size were similar across all tested genotypes (Figure 4C,D, Figure 4—figure supplement 4C–E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 4C–E

claim: Abnormal eye-specific segregation was not observed in either melanopsin knockout mice (Opn4LacZ/LacZ) or mice with ipRGCs ablated during adulthood (Opn4aDTA/aDTA).
source: Abnormal eye-specific segregation was not observed in either melanopsin knockout mice (Opn4LacZ/LacZ) or mice with ipRGCs ablated during adulthood (Opn4aDTA/aDTA) (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A–D

claim: Opn4DTA/+ mice exhibited disrupted eye-specific segregation that was intermediate between wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA mice.
source: Importantly, Opn4DTA/+ mice, which have substantial ipRGC loss, although to lesser degree than Opn4DTA/DTA mice, exhibited disrupted eye-specific segregation that was intermediate between wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA mice (Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 4F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 4F

claim: ipRGCs have a developmental role in the segregation of all RGC inputs to the dLGN.
source: Combined, these data reveal an developmental role for ipRGCs in the segregation of all RGC inputs to the dLGN.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ipRGC ablation disrupts eye-specific segregation

claim: Eye-specific segregation deficits in Opn4DTA/DTA mice were observed by P8.
source: To conclusively determine whether ipRGCs function during early postnatal ages to regulate refinement of retinogeniculate projections, we examined eye-specific segregation at P8 and, similar to adult mice, found an increase in overlapping ipsilateral and contralateral projections in Opn4DTA/DTA mice, but no difference in total retinal input compared to wild-type (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5A–D

claim: ipRGCs function at early postnatal ages to mediate refinement of the image-forming visual system by regulating eye-specific segregation of retinogeniculate projections.
source: These data indicate that ipRGCs function at early postnatal ages to mediate refinement of the image-forming visual system by regulating eye-specific segregation of retinogeniculate projections.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of segregation deficits at P8 in Opn4DTA/DTA mice

claim: Opn4DTA/DTA animals exhibited reduced visual acuity compared to controls (wild-type and Opn4LacZ/LacZ) by both the virtual optomotor system and the visual water task.
source: To examine the functional consequence of altered eye-specific segregation, we compared wild-type, Opn4LacZ/LacZ, and Opn4DTA/DTA mice in two behavioral tests of visual acuity: the virtual optomotor system and the visual water task (Douglas et al., 2005; Prusky et al., 2000). By both measures, Opn4DTA/DTA animals exhibited reduced visual acuity compared to controls (wild-type and Opn4LacZ/LacZ; Figure 4E,F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4E,F

claim: Opn4DTA/+ mice exhibited an intermediate reduction in visual acuity compared to wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA mice.
source: Remarkably, Opn4DTA/+ mice also exhibited an intermediate reduction in visual acuity (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4E,F

claim: The severity of the deficits in eye-specific segregation and visual functions were correlated with the extent of ipRGC loss.
source: Thus, the severity of the deficits in eye-specific segregation and visual functions were correlated with the extent of ipRGC loss.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of phenotypes across genotypes with different degrees of ipRGC loss

claim: Spiking properties of RGCs during waves were significantly altered in Opn4DTA/DTA mice.
source: Spiking properties of RGCs during waves were significantly altered in Opn4DTA/DTA mice. Wave-associated bursts (WABs) were significantly longer in duration, and had higher firing rates, and shorter inter-burst intervals (Figure 5E,G–H, Supplementary file 2) than they did in wild-type controls.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5E,G–H and Supplementary file 2

claim: Wave-associated bursts (WABs) were significantly longer in duration in Opn4DTA/DTA mice compared to wild-type controls.
source: Wave-associated bursts (WABs) were significantly longer in duration, and had higher firing rates, and shorter inter-burst intervals (Figure 5E,G–H, Supplementary file 2) than they did in wild-type controls.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5E,G–H and Supplementary file 2

claim: WABs had higher firing rates in Opn4DTA/DTA mice compared to wild-type controls.
source: Wave-associated bursts (WABs) were significantly longer in duration, and had higher firing rates, and shorter inter-burst intervals (Figure 5E,G–H, Supplementary file 2) than they did in wild-type controls.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5E,G–H and Supplementary file 2

claim: WABs had shorter inter-burst intervals in Opn4DTA/DTA mice compared to wild-type controls.
source: Wave-associated bursts (WABs) were significantly longer in duration, and had higher firing rates, and shorter inter-burst intervals (Figure 5E,G–H, Supplementary file 2) than they did in wild-type controls.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5E,G–H and Supplementary file 2

claim: There were significantly more total spikes as well as more spikes outside of bursts in Opn4DTA/DTA mice compared to wild-type controls.
source: There were also significantly more total spikes as well as more spikes outside of bursts (Figure 5E,G–H, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5E,G–H and Supplementary file 2

claim: Correlated spiking activity between neurons was very similar between wild-type and Opn4DTA/DTA genotypes.
source: Correlated spiking activity between neurons was very similar between the genotypes, as measured by the spike time tiling coefficient (STTC; [Cutts and Eglen, 2014])(Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5F

claim: ipRGCs are critical for normal retinal wave activity, even in darkness.
source: These data indicate that ipRGCs are critical for normal retinal wave activity, even in darkness, and together with our anatomical findings (Figure 4A–D; Figure 4—figure supplements 3–4), allow us to suggest that ipRGCs mediate eye-specific segregation of RGC projections to the dLGN by regulating the spiking properties of conventional RGCs during retinal waves.
evidence: Inferred from the altered retinal wave properties in Opn4DTA/DTA mice

claim: ipRGCs mediate eye-specific segregation of RGC projections to the dLGN by regulating the spiking properties of conventional RGCs during retinal waves.
source: These data indicate that ipRGCs are critical for normal retinal wave activity, even in darkness, and together with our anatomical findings (Figure 4A–D; Figure 4—figure supplements 3–4), allow us to suggest that ipRGCs mediate eye-specific segregation of RGC projections to the dLGN by regulating the spiking properties of conventional RGCs during retinal waves.
evidence: Suggested mechanism based on combined anatomical and electrophysiological findings

claim: There are currently five identified subtypes of ipRGCs.
source: There are currently five identified subtypes of ipRGCs.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field

claim: M1 ipRGCs project to non-image-forming brain centers, while M2-M5 ipRGCs project at least in part to image-forming targets.
source: M1 ipRGCs project to non-image-forming brain centers, while M2-M5 ipRGCs project at least in part to image-forming targets (Ecker et al., 2010; Schmidt et al., 2011; Schmidt and Kofuji, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ecker et al., 2010; Schmidt et al., 2011; Schmidt and Kofuji, 2009

claim: The M1 subtype can be further subdivided based on expression of the transcription factor Pou4f2 (also referred to as Brn3b), which is also expressed in all non-M1 ipRGCs.
source: The M1 subtype can be further subdivided based on expression of the transcription factor Pou4f2 (also referred to as Brn3b), which is also expressed in all non-M1 ipRGCs (Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2011

claim: ~200 Pou4f2-negative-M1 ipRGCs project exclusively to circadian centers (predominantly to the SCN).
source: ~200 Pou4f2-negative-M1 ipRGCs project exclusively to circadian centers (predominantly to the SCN) (Figure 4—figure supplement 5B) (Chen et al., 2011) and are the subset of ipRGCs that have intra-retinal collateral axons (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2011 and data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5B

claim: Light plays an essential role in setting the circadian period.

evidence: Inferred from the dark-rearing experiments showing light-dependent effects on period but not segregation

claim: Light does not play an essential role in the image-forming visual process of eye-specific segregation.

claim: ipRGCs constitute a shared node in the neural circuits that mediate light-dependent maturation of the circadian clock and refinement of retinogeniculate projections.

evidence: Inferred from the combined findings showing ipRGC involvement in both processes
